stem: An employee receives a phone call from someone claiming to be from the IT service desk, asking them to read out the code that just arrived on their phone. What is this?

options.text: Vishing
options.why: The channel is a voice call, which makes it vishing, and the goal is to defeat the second factor.

options.text: Phishing
options.why: Technically part of the phishing family, and the exam wants the channel specific term when the channel is stated.

options.text: Smishing
options.why: Smishing arrives by SMS. The code arrived by SMS, the attack arrived by phone call.

options.text: Whaling
options.why: Whaling targets an executive. Nothing indicates the employee is one.

stem: Finance receives an email from the CFO's genuine mailbox, in their usual style, asking for an urgent wire transfer to a new account. Mail authentication passes because the message really did come from that mailbox. What is this?

options.text: Business email compromise
options.why: The attacker controls a real, legitimate mailbox, which is why SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass and the message reads as authentic.

options.text: Whaling
options.why: Whaling targets an executive. Here the executive's account is the weapon, and finance staff are the target.

options.text: Spoofing
options.why: Nothing is spoofed. The message genuinely originates from the CFO's account, which is what makes it so effective.

options.text: Smishing
options.why: The channel is email, not SMS.

stem: An attacker compromises a managed service provider and uses its remote management tooling to deploy ransomware to 200 of its clients simultaneously. Which risk does this illustrate?

options.text: Third-party and supply chain risk through a service provider's privileged access
options.why: The MSP holds trusted administrative access into every client, so compromising it once reaches all of them.

options.text: Insider threat at each of the 200 clients
options.why: No client employee acted. The trusted access came from outside each organisation.

options.text: Shadow IT
options.why: The MSP relationship is sanctioned and contracted, which is the opposite of shadow IT.

options.text: A zero-day in the clients' endpoint protection
options.why: The deployment used legitimate management tooling with legitimate credentials, so no exploit was needed.

stem: Staff at an engineering firm are compromised after visiting a small industry standards site they all read daily. The site itself was breached a week earlier and now serves a malicious script to visitors from that firm's address range. Which threat vector is this?

options.text: A watering hole attack
options.why: The attacker compromised a site the target population is already known to visit, then waited. No message was sent to anyone.

options.text: Typosquatting
options.why: Typosquatting registers a lookalike domain and relies on a mistyped address. Here the victims reached exactly the site they meant to visit.

options.text: Brand impersonation
options.why: Brand impersonation forges the appearance of a trusted organisation. The site here was genuine and genuinely compromised, which is why nothing looked wrong.

options.text: Business email compromise
options.why: BEC runs through a real or spoofed mailbox to push a transaction. No email was involved in this chain.

stem: A vulnerability review finds a reporting service reachable on the network whose web console still accepts the vendor's shipped administrator password. No user interaction is needed to exploit it. Which description fits the vector best?

options.text: An open service port exposing software with default credentials
options.why: The opening is the exposed service plus an unchanged shipped credential. It is reached directly, with nobody tricked into anything.

options.text: A message-based vector, because the console is reached over the web
options.why: Message-based means a human is addressed and asked to act: email, SMS, instant message, voice call. Browsing to a service is not that.

options.text: A supply chain vector, because the vendor shipped the password
options.why: Supply chain means the attacker uses trust you extended to a supplier. Here the vendor's default is simply a configuration you failed to change on your own estate.

options.text: A zero-day, because no patch has been applied
options.why: Nothing is unknown to the vendor here and no patch is missing. A password that was never changed is a hardening failure, not a vulnerability awaiting a fix.

stem: During a product recall, coordinated accounts post fabricated claims that a company's safety certificates were withdrawn. Share price falls and the support desk is overwhelmed. Nothing on the company network is touched. Which best describes what is being used against the company?

options.text: A misinformation and disinformation campaign
options.why: The objectives list this as a human vector in its own right. The asset under attack is trust, and no system has to be breached to damage it.

options.text: Brand impersonation
options.why: Brand impersonation means posing as the company. These accounts are speaking about the company, not pretending to be it.

options.text: A denial of service attack
options.why: The support desk is overwhelmed by real people reacting to a story. No traffic is being directed at a service to exhaust it.

options.text: Pretexting
options.why: Pretexting builds a false scenario to extract something from a specific target. This is broadcast, and it asks nobody for anything.

stem: A USB drive labelled 'Q3 salaries' is found in the car park. An employee plugs it in and opens the spreadsheet on it, which runs a macro. Which threat vector did the attacker use to get the payload onto the workstation?

options.text: Removable device: the drive crossing the boundary is the route in
options.why: The vector is how the attacker first reached the machine. Physical media carried across the perimeter is the removable device vector; everything after that is payload.

options.text: Email, because the labelled drive works like a phishing lure
options.why: No message was sent. A lure can ride any vector; this one was physical.

options.text: File-based, because the macro in the spreadsheet is the weapon
options.why: File-based describes the payload. The question asked how it got onto the workstation, and the stem says so.

options.text: Vulnerable software, because the spreadsheet application ran the macro
options.why: Nothing was exploited. The application did what it was asked to do by a user who opened the file.

stem: An attacker gains a foothold through a building management controller running an operating system whose vendor ended support four years ago. No credential was guessed and no user was tricked. Which threat vector is this?

options.text: Unsupported system: a weakness that will never be patched
options.why: The stem rules out credentials and people and names an end-of-support system. That is the unsupported systems and applications vector.

options.text: Default credentials
options.why: The stem says no credential was guessed. Default credentials are a configuration the attacker logs in with; nothing was logged into here.

options.text: Vulnerable software with a patch available
options.why: A supported system with a patch waiting is vulnerable software. One whose vendor ended support can never be patched, which is why the exam lists it separately and why it is the worse case.

options.text: Pretexting against the facilities team
options.why: No one was tricked. Pretexting needs a person to believe a story.

stem: A visitor in reception plugs a laptop into a wall socket behind a plant and receives an internal address. Which threat vector is this, and which control closes it?

options.text: Unsecure wired network; enable 802.1X on the switch ports or disable the unused ones
options.why: A live jack in a public area is the unsecure wired vector, and port authentication or shutting the port is the control that closes exactly that opening.

options.text: Unsecure wireless network; move the access points to WPA3
options.why: The visitor used a cable. WPA3 closes a wireless opening and leaves this one wide open.

options.text: Bluetooth; set devices to non-discoverable
options.why: No pairing happened. Bluetooth is a device-to-device opening, not a wall socket.

options.text: Open service port; close the port on the server
options.why: A switch port is a physical jack. An open service port is a listening service on a host, a different opening with a different fix.

stem: Three organisations are breached in the same week. In the first, a firmware update signed by the maker of their firewalls carried a backdoor. In the second, an attacker used a remote management tool's credentials to reach dozens of client networks at once. In the third, network cards bought for a new data centre arrived with modified firmware. Which supply chain vectors are these, in order?

options.text: Vendor, managed service provider, supplier
options.why: A product's own update is the vendor; standing remote access across many clients is an MSP; tampered components arriving upstream is a supplier.

options.text: Supplier, vendor, managed service provider
options.why: The firewall maker sold a finished product, which makes them a vendor; the component maker is the supplier; the remote tool with standing access is the MSP.

options.text: Vendor, vendor, vendor
options.why: The exam separates them because each is closed differently: vendor updates by validation, MSP access by least privilege and monitoring, supplier components by inspection before deployment.

options.text: Managed service provider, supplier, vendor
options.why: A signed firmware update is the product vendor's, and the remote management tool reaching many clients at once is the signature of an MSP.

stem: Staff receive a text message with a link to 'reset your expiring password'. Which threat vector and which attack are these?

options.text: SMS; smishing
options.why: A text message is the SMS vector, and phishing over SMS is smishing.

options.text: Instant messaging; phishing
options.why: The stem names a text message. Instant messaging is a different message vector with a different name for the attack.

options.text: Voice call; vishing
options.why: Nobody called. Vishing is phishing by voice.

options.text: Email; phishing
options.why: Phishing is defensible as the family, but the channel named is SMS, and the exam wants the precise term.

stem: A domain one character away from the company's own hosts a login page copied from the real one, and the address is circulated in posts claiming the company has been breached. Which technique best describes the domain itself?

options.text: Typosquatting
options.why: A near-miss domain registered to catch mistypes and look legitimate is typosquatting. The page it serves and the posts promoting it are other techniques.

options.text: Brand impersonation
options.why: The copied login page is brand impersonation. The question asked about the domain, and the one-character-off address is the typosquatting part.

options.text: Disinformation
options.why: The breach posts are disinformation. The domain is a counterfeit address, not a false claim.

options.text: Watering hole
options.why: A watering hole compromises a legitimate site the targets already visit. This is a lure to a site the attacker built.

stem: During a merger announcement an employee forwards an article to the whole company that falsely claims the deal has collapsed; the employee believed it. Separately, an account styled as the chief executive's posts the same claim with fabricated figures. Which is misinformation and which is disinformation?

options.text: The forward is misinformation; the posts are disinformation
options.why: The employee spread a falsehood in good faith, which is misinformation. The fabricated, impersonating posts were made to deceive, which is disinformation.

options.text: Both are disinformation
options.why: Disinformation is deliberate. The employee believed the article, so their forward is misinformation.

options.text: Both are misinformation
options.why: Fabricated figures under a counterfeit identity are deliberate deception. That is disinformation.

options.text: The forward is impersonation; the posts are misinformation
options.why: The employee impersonated nobody. The posts are the impersonation, and their content is disinformation.

stem: An attacker embeds a script inside an SVG image attached to an email. The script runs when the image is previewed. The question asks which vector carries the payload. Which is it?

options.text: Image-based
options.why: The image is the carrier. Email delivered it, but the stem asks what carries the payload, and an image with executable content inside it is the image-based vector.

options.text: Email, because that is what arrived
options.why: Email is the delivery channel. When the stem asks what carries the payload rather than how it was delivered, it is asking for the file or image vector.

options.text: Vulnerable software, because the preview rendered it
options.why: Rendering an image is the software working as designed. Nothing was exploited; the content did the work.

options.text: Removable device
options.why: Nothing physical crossed the boundary. The image arrived over the network.

stem: An organisation outsources monitoring of its firewalls to a third party that holds administrative credentials and connects through a remote management agent. The third party is breached. Which threat vector is this, and what makes it more dangerous than a compromised software vendor?

options.text: Managed service provider; it holds standing privileged access, so the breach reaches you without any update or user action
options.why: An MSP operates your systems with credentials you granted. Their attacker is already inside, which a vendor's attacker is not until you install something.

options.text: Vendor; the danger is the same as any compromised product
options.why: A vendor sold a product; it reaches you when you take an update. An MSP already has the keys, which is a different and faster route.

options.text: Supplier; the agent is a component they supplied
options.why: A supplier provides parts that go into what you run. The agent is the MSP's access path, not a component of your product.

options.text: Insider threat; the credentials belong to an internal account
options.why: Access you granted to an outside party is a supply chain vector. The people using it are not your employees.

stem: A hospital buys infusion pumps from a medical device manufacturer. Investigators find that the pumps' wireless modules, made by a separate company and fitted during manufacture, shipped with a hidden debug account. Which supply chain party introduced the weakness?

options.text: The vendor, because the hospital bought the pumps from them
options.why: The manufacturer is the vendor and is accountable for what it ships, but the question asks where the weakness entered. It entered with a component from another firm.

options.text: The supplier of the wireless module, a component that arrived already inside the product
options.why: The weakness came in with a part made by another company and built into the finished device. That is the supplier vector: tampered or flawed components inside what you bought.

options.text: A managed service provider, because the pumps connect over wireless
options.why: An MSP operates something for you with standing access. Nobody here runs the pumps on the hospital's behalf; a wireless connection is not a service provider.

options.text: An insider at the hospital who configured the pumps
options.why: The account existed before the pumps arrived. Nothing in the stem points to anyone at the hospital creating it.

stem: A competitor pays a network of accounts to post fabricated claims that a company's mobile app leaks customer data. Thousands of ordinary users, believing the claims, repost them to warn their friends. How should the paid posts and the reposts be classified?

options.text: Both are disinformation, because the claim is false
options.why: Falsity alone does not make disinformation. The users reposting it believed it and meant to help, which is misinformation.

options.text: Both are misinformation, because the claim is false
options.why: The accounts were paid to post something they knew was invented. Deliberate falsehood is disinformation.

options.text: The paid posts are disinformation; the reposts are misinformation
options.why: The same falsehood is deliberate in the hands of the people who invented it and innocent in the hands of the people who believed it. Intent is the whole distinction.

options.text: The paid posts are brand impersonation; the reposts are disinformation
options.why: Nothing is pretending to be the company; the posts attack it. And the users reposting in good faith are not acting deliberately.

stem: A tester sitting in the car park finds that the conference room speakerphones accept pairing requests from any nearby device without confirmation. Which threat vector is this, and which control closes it?

options.text: Unsecure wireless network; move the corporate network to WPA3
options.why: WPA3 protects the Wi-Fi network. The speakerphones are accepting Bluetooth pairings, which WPA3 never touches.

options.text: Unsecure wired network; enable 802.1X on the conference room switch ports
options.why: 802.1X controls which devices may use a cable. The tester never plugged anything in.

options.text: Default credentials; change the speakerphones' administrator passwords
options.why: No password was used. The devices accept a pairing without asking for anything, so a new password changes nothing.

options.text: Bluetooth; make the devices non-discoverable and require confirmation for every pairing
options.why: The opening is a short-range radio accepting strangers. The control that closes exactly that opening is on the pairing itself.
